messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lukas, a 19-year-old counselor, still shudders at the memory of the hospital smell that clings to his clothes after every visit. The antiseptic scent transports him back to the months he spent in and out of hospitals, battling a life-threatening illness that left him feeling like his body had betrayed him. His eyes dart towards any medical equipment within sight – needles, drips, or even just the hospital's sleek architecture – triggering an overwhelming urge to flee. Lukas has developed an arsenal of avoidance strategies to cope with these triggers. He steers clear of discussing anything related to his illness in therapy sessions, changing the subject whenever it comes up. At night, he stays up until the early hours, delaying sleep as a way to avoid the nightmares that inevitably follow. Hospitals, ambulances, and even physical examinations are strictly off-limits – the mere thought of them sends his heart racing. As Lukas navigates these landmines, he finds himself constantly on edge, bracing for danger at every turn. Unexpected movements nearby make him jump, and his body reacts as if he's still in harm's way, even when logic tells him otherwise. The sleep problems that plague him only exacerbate this hyper-vigilance, leaving him perpetually exhausted and irritable. Lukas has come to believe that his illness has irreparably shattered the trust between him and his own body. He feels lost and without direction, as if nothing in life holds any meaning anymore. His body's continued reactivity – the way it betrays him with a racing heart or trembling hands at the slightest provocation – only reinforces this sense of betrayal. Lukas is certain that his body remains stuck in danger mode, perpetually primed for a threat that no longer exists. This toxic dynamic has Lukas trapped in a vicious cycle. His negative appraisals of himself and his body drive him to avoid confronting his fears, which in turn strengthens the very triggers he's trying to evade. As he struggles to make sense of this chaos, Lukas finds himself questioning whether he'll ever be able to break free from this cycle of avoidance and reactivity. Despite his best efforts, Lukas can't shake off the feeling that his body is still responding to a threat that's long gone – every creak of the floorboards or distant siren makes him flinch. His sleep-deprived brain struggles to distinguish between what's real and what's just his hyper-vigilant imagination running wild. Lukas knows he needs help, but it's hard for him to admit it – especially given his role as a counselor, where vulnerability feels like a luxury he can't afford. Still, the exhaustion and fear that have taken over his life finally brought him to seek help. As he begins this journey, Lukas hopes to learn how to trust himself again, to find meaning in a world that still feels overwhelming – and perhaps, just perhaps, to silence the constant alarm blaring within him.
